prompt:
A photograph taken inside the great hall of an English castle that is open to visitors, in the flat daylight coming through the hall windows. High on the stone wall, four painted family shields hang side by side.

Each shield is done the same way: one flat tincture over the whole face, and one single figure laid over it, also in one flat tincture. The four figures, one to a shield, are a lion, an eagle, a cross and a chevron. Every one of the eight tinctures must be one a herald is entitled to use, and no shield may carry any tincture beyond its own two.

The visitors' plaque under the shields carries this text and nothing else:
FOUR SHIELDS OF THE HOUSE, HUNG HERE SINCE 1614. THREE WERE CHECKED AGAINST THE OLD RULE OF TINCTURE BY THE COLLEGE OF ARMS. ONE WAS REPAINTED IN 1872 BY A DECORATOR WHO HAD NEVER HEARD OF THE RULE.

The room guides stand at this wall and teach the oldest rule of the trade off it, so the wall has to bear out what the plaque says. Choose the eight tinctures yourself -- I am deliberately not telling you what the rule is, which tinctures may lie over which, or which of the four is the 1872 shield. No tincture name, no heraldic term, no shield number and no writing of any kind may appear anywhere in the picture apart from the plaque text above.

All four shields and the plaque must be in the same frame, and each shield's two tinctures must be unmistakable.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show four painted shields hanging in a row on a wall with a plaque under them? A realistic photo, an illustration, a schematic or a clean diagram ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image instead shows just a blank card or plain panel that prints an answer with none of that shown, or shows something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.
